title: Detection Strategy for Modify System Image on Network Devices
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for Modify System Image on Network Dev...
summary: This strategy covers modification of the system image on network devices, which means replacing or altering the firmware or operating system image that a router, switch or firewall boots and runs. Because the change happens outside the endpoint operating system, ordinary endpoint telemetry never sees it; the evidence lives in device configuration and image management logs, in the authentication records of administrators who reach the device, and in file transfer records for image uploads. An analyst detects it by correlating an image or boot variable change with the administrator account, source address and maintenance window that produced it. The common failure is weak or missing logging on network gear, which leaves the change visible only after a reboot surprises everyone.

beginner.definition: Network devices such as routers and switches run software called firmware or a system image. This detection looks for someone replacing or changing that image. It catches tampering that normal computer monitoring cannot see.
beginner.whyItMatters: The image is the most trusted part of a network device. If it is changed, every packet the device handles can be watched or altered. Endpoint tools do not monitor these devices, so the change can stay hidden for months. Rebuilding a device is slow and costly. Catching the upload early avoids all of this.
howItWorks: Administrators reach network devices in two main ways. They use a management session such as Secure Shell, or they load a file through a transfer service such as Trivial File Transfer Protocol.
The device, or the server that controls access, writes a record of each login. The record includes the account name, the source address and the time.
The device also writes configuration change records when the boot image setting or a stored image file is changed.
The detection links an image upload or boot setting change to the administrator session that happened just before it.
It then compares that account, address and time with the approved change window and the list of people allowed to perform it.
Anything outside that approved pattern is raised for review before the next reboot.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital sign-in sheet at the pharmacy. Anyone can walk past the counter, but only listed staff may collect a controlled drug, and each collection is written down. If a name appears that is not on the list, or at three in the morning, staff investigate before the drugs leave the room.
takeaways: Network device firmware lives below your endpoint tools, so you need device and authentication logs.
The strong signal is an image change tied to an unexpected account, address or time.
You cannot detect this at all on devices that do not log administrative sessions.

objectives: Describe what a network device system image is and why changing it affects all traffic through the device
List the telemetry sources that can show an image upload or boot variable change on network hardware
Correlate an administrative authentication event with a subsequent image or configuration change
Compare observed change activity against approved change windows and authorised administrator accounts
Identify which network assets lack adequate logging and prioritise them for improvement
dataSources: Network device configuration change logs recording boot system variable changes and image file operations
TACACS+ or RADIUS authentication and command accounting records for administrative sessions on network hardware
Secure Shell and console session logs from the device management plane including source address and account name
File transfer service logs showing image file uploads to network device management addresses
Change management tickets used to compare approved maintenance windows with observed image changes
logic: The detection looks for an image or boot variable change on a network device that cannot be matched to an approved change record and an authorised administrative session. The fields that matter are the device identity, the account that authenticated, the source address of that session, the exact change or upload event and its timestamp, because any one of them alone is normal on its own. A benign case is a scheduled firmware upgrade performed by a named network engineer from a jump host inside an agreed window, with a matching ticket. The malicious case typically shows an interactive management session from an unusual address or account, followed within minutes by an image upload or boot loader change, often outside a maintenance window, and sometimes with logging disabled on the same device shortly before.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Network Device System Image Modified Outside Change Window
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     action:
#       - image_upload
#       - boot_variable_change
#       - copy_run_start
#   filter:
#     account|in: approved_network_admins
#     src_ip|in: jump_host_ranges
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: high
falsePositives: A scheduled firmware upgrade performed by the network team from the jump host during an approved maintenance window
Disaster recovery testing that reimages lab or standby routers outside normal business hours with a change ticket
A vendor support engineer loading a patched image remotely under a logged support case
Automated configuration backups that briefly copy a running configuration to a startup location
tuningNotes: Build a baseline of every account and source address that normally authenticates to network devices, and maintain a live list of approved maintenance windows from the change system so the rule can suppress matching activity automatically. Scope the rule first to core routing, firewall and virtual private network concentrators, because those carry the most traffic and the biggest impact, then extend to access switches once alert quality is proven. Filtering by account and jump host removes the bulk of noise but loses coverage of abuse by a compromised legitimate administrator account, so keep an unfiltered version at lower severity for those accounts and review it during investigations.
